item.title: A quantitative framework for evaluating marine-based geologic constraints on Antarctic Ice Sheet retreat
item.dc:creator: Anna Ruth W. Halberstadt, Ryan A. Venturelli, Lindsay O. Prothro, T. M. King, Sara C. Peters
item.description:
Quaternary Science Reviews — matched: ice sheet, ice-sheet modelling, grounding line, Antarctic, deglaciation, sediment core, radiocarbon, sea level, sea-level rise, solid earth, numerical method, ensemble
Reconstructing Antarctic Ice Sheet evolution through the last deglaciation is crucial for quantifying global sea level rise and solid Earth loading changes. This endeavor requires both empirical geologic observations and numerical ice sheet models: geologic data offer valuable but spatially and temporally fragmented snapshots of past glacial configurations, whereas numerical models provide three-dimensional physically based ice evolution but generate a wide range of plausible deglacial histories. Together, these approaches enable process-level insights into ice sheet sensitivity to warmth. Here we focus on the marine seafloor, combining geologic information gleaned from sediment cores and mapped seafloor landforms with numerical ice sheet modeling. We develop model-data comparison metrics that assess both the timing of grounding-line recession and its spatial pattern across the Amundsen and Ross Sea continental shelves. The application of these metrics to a targeted ensemble of ice sheet model simulations demonstrates the power of geologic data to constrain the chronology and amplitude of modeled deglacial ice loss. Marine radiocarbon and seafloor landform observations are translated into glaciologically consistent reconstructions of regional ice sheet deglaciation, lending quantitative context for the reconstruction of low-slope ice sheets that remain pinned on seafloor highs as deglaciation progresses. This work highlights the use of physically self-consistent ice sheet models as a powerful tool to contextualize geologic records of Antarctic deglaciation.

item.title: Observed fingerprint of global warming exposes model biases in regional climate attribution
item.dc:creator: Hasi Aru, Dirk Olonscheck, Jochem Marotzke, Chao Li
item.description:
Science Advances — matched: Arctic, CMIP, ensemble, global warming
Disentangling externally forced signals from internal variability in observed surface air temperature (SAT) is essential for reliable regional climate detection and attribution. Although climate model simulated patterns broadly align with observed global warming, persistent regional discrepancies, compounded by the limitation of a single observational realization, impede robust regional attribution. We identify the observation-based SAT externally forced signals and internal variability, which allows us to compare the observed SAT patterns with the simulated counterparts from seven CMIP6 single-model initial-condition large ensembles. Perfect-model tests confirm robust large-scale partitioning, while indicating reduced fidelity where internal variability dominates. Our results suggest that models tend to overestimate emergence timescales in externally forced regions but underestimate them in internal variability–dominated regions. In several internal variability–dominated regions, the forced signal remains undetectable in observations. While Arctic warming is increasingly dominated by external forcing, internal variability has slowed its rate in recent decades. In internal variability–dominated regions, we identify modest yet consistent externally forced contributions, with observed cooling trends and sign flips primarily driven by internal variability. These findings help to resolve long-standing regional attribution puzzles, highlight critical model limitations, and carry fundamental implications for regional climate projections, attribution, and jurisprudence.

item.title: Farmers’ Perspectives on Climate Change and Heat Stress Adaptation in Rural Zambia: A Just Transformations Approach
item.dc:creator: Anayawa Nyambe
item.description:
Sustainability and Climate Change — matched: climate change
Climate change adaptation projects and initiatives are increasingly being implemented in rural farming communities. These initiatives have the potential to assist small-scale farmers in confronting environmental and social issues and health-related challenges, such as heat stress. However, questions remain regarding their effectiveness, inclusivity, and long-term sustainability. This study examined farmers’ perspectives on climate change and heat-stress adaptation initiatives in Zambia using the Just Transformations Framework. Focus group discussions supported by photo elicitation were conducted among small-scale farmers in Monze and Sioma Districts. Farmers described experiencing reduced agricultural productivity and changing weather patterns. They identified a range of adaptation responses, including reforestation, stricter regulation of charcoal and timber production, Indigenous Knowledge practices that aid heat stress prevention (e.g., traditional water coolers), and support from government and non-governmental stakeholders. While some participants acknowledged the value of climate-related projects and interventions, many raised concerns about limited inclusivity, bureaucratic barriers, and unequal access to resources and project benefits. Findings also revealed a gap between externally designed projects and the priorities identified by local communities. Consequently, farmers reported that climate change initiatives often fail to address their most urgent needs or provide visible benefits at household level. This study emphasizes the importance of justice-oriented and community-driven approaches in the design and implementation of climate change initiatives. Greater attention to local priorities, participation, and equity is essential for ensuring that climate interventions are effective, sustainable, and responsive to local contexts.
